case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: G.S. v. Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the 'minimum degree of care' in N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4) means grossly or wantonly negligent conduct, not ordinary negligence, and affirmed the neglect finding against a caregiver who recklessly over-medicated a child.
key_cases.relevance: G.S. arose from a serious medication injury to a child in a group-home setting and defines when such an injury is legally neglect.
key_cases.quote: the phrase "minimum degree of care" refers to conduct that is grossly or wantonly negligent, but not necessarily intentional

key_cases.case_name: L.A. v. New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services
key_cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
key_cases.holding: The court defined the standard governing a physician's statutory duty to report, holding 'reasonable cause to believe' exists when a probable inference from the available information is that the child's condition results from abuse.
key_cases.relevance: L.A. arose from civil claims after a child was seriously injured following an unreported or under-investigated presentation.
key_cases.quote: The inference need not be the "most probable," but it must be more than speculation or suspicion.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held the Due Process Clause imposed no constitutional duty on the county to protect a child from his father's violence, even though the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial or other special relationship.
key_cases.relevance: DeShaney governs the federal claims that follow a child's death or serious injury in an open agency case.
key_cases.quote: the Due Process Clauses generally confer no affirmative right to governmental aid, even where such aid may be necessary to secure life, liberty, or property interests
